lead: The TCP/IP protocol suite defines the practical Internet. It groups functions into four layers. Each layer hides details from the one above. The model lets devices from any vendor interoperate. It is used in every web, email, and mobile transaction across India.

blocks.text: The TCP/IP suite has four layers: Application, Transport, Internet, and Link. The Application layer hosts protocols such as HTTP, DNS, and SMTP. The Transport layer provides end‑to‑end services using TCP or UDP. The Internet layer routes packets with IPv4 or IPv6. The Link layer moves frames over a physical medium like Ethernet or Wi‑Fi.

The layers map to the OSI model. Application roughly covers OSI layers 5–7. Transport matches OSI layer 4. Internet corresponds to OSI layer 3. Link aligns with OSI layers 1–2. Some syllabi call this mapping the Internet architecture.

items: Application – user data and protocol semantics

blocks.text: IPv4 uses a 32‑bit address written as four decimal octets. It has a 20‑byte header for basic services. IPv6 expands the address to 128 bits and uses a fixed 40‑byte header. IPv6 includes optional IPsec support for security and, because of its large address space, typically eliminates the need for NAT, though NAT may still be employed in specific scenarios.
Routers make routing decisions at the Internet layer by examining the destination IP address, but they also handle Link‑layer frames to forward packets on the appropriate physical link.

items: Both carry source and destination addresses

blocks.text: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery. It adds a 20‑byte header containing source and destination ports, sequence number, acknowledgment number, data offset, flags, window size, checksum, and urgent pointer. UDP offers connectionless service with a 8‑byte header and no retransmission.
Application protocols use these transport services. A web browser sends an HTTP GET request over TCP. An online game may use UDP to reduce latency.

items: Transport encapsulates payload in a segment.
Internet encapsulates segment in a packet.
Link encapsulates packet in a frame.

examples.question: A client sends a 500 B HTTP request over Ethernet. The TCP header is 20 B, the IPv4 header is 20 B, and the Ethernet header is 14 B. Compute the total number of bytes transmitted on the wire.
steps: Add TCP header: 500 B + 20 B = 520 B.
Add IPv4 header: 520 B + 20 B = 540 B.
Add Ethernet header: 540 B + 14 B = 554 B.
Add Ethernet CRC: 554 B + 4 B = 558 B.
examples.answer: The total size on the wire is 558 B.
examples.check:
payload = 500
tcp_hdr = 20
ip_hdr = 20
eth_hdr = 14
crc = 4
total = payload + tcp_hdr + ip_hdr + eth_hdr + crc
print(total)

traps: Assuming the IPv6 header is 20 B. It is actually 40 B.
Adding only one header size and forgetting the Ethernet frame.
Treating the payload as already including the TCP header.
Confusing bits with bytes when converting IP address lengths.
Using the term "layer 2" for the Application layer.

quiz.q: Name the four layers of the TCP/IP model in order from top to bottom.
Explain why the Internet layer is highlighted in the TCP/IP stack figure.
quiz.a: It performs logical addressing and routing, which are central to moving packets across different networks.

quiz.q: A packet carries a 300 B payload, a TCP header of 20 B and an IPv4 header of 20 B. What is the size of the IP packet before it enters the Link layer?
If an IPv6 packet has a 1000 B payload, what is the total size of the IPv6 packet (header + payload)?
quiz.a: IPv6 header = 40 B, so total = 40 B + 1000 B = 1040 B.

quiz.q: Compare TCP and UDP in terms of reliability, header size, and typical use cases.
quiz.a: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery with a 20 B header; used for web, email, file transfer. UDP offers best‑effort delivery with an 8 B header; used for streaming, gaming, DNS.

quiz.q: Which OSI layer corresponds most closely to the TCP/IP Transport layer?
Why does the TCP/IP model have fewer layers than the OSI model?
quiz.a: It combines OSI layers 5–7 into a single Application layer and merges layers 1–2 into a Link layer for simplicity.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the TCP/IP stack is extended with TLS for security and QUIC for low‑latency transport. Research explores IPv6 adoption barriers and programmable data planes using P4. New curricula add SDN concepts that treat the Internet layer as a software‑controlled entity. Search for "TCP/IP performance tuning" and "IPv6 transition mechanisms" for deeper study.
